title: This game is 100% AI Engineered
author: EnzeDfu
selftext:
Hello everyone! One month ago, I decided to put my AI coding skills to the challenge and  take upon one of the most difficult genre to code: automation games like Factorio.

That's how **Zombies Per Minute** was born! It is a factory-building roguelite where everything you build is measured by one thing: how many zombies you can kill per minute. Yes, really.

As of now, I spent around one month on it (somwhere around 150 hours I would say).

I used only 2 AI Agents:

\- GPT-5.3-Codex for 80% of the task, mostly logics, simulation, render, performance

\- Opus 4.6 in Claude Code for frontend and UI (I think it has more taste than Codex)

  
For sound and music, I went with ElevenLabs.

For 3D, everything is made programmatically with primitives, except the character (mixamo for now) and the zombies from Quaternius).

Regarding the tech stack, I went with Vite + React + TypeScript (I found the LLM so good with TS), and the library is ThreeJS, more precisely React Three Fiber.

It's been SO HARD to optimize for performance, as it is a web game and there can be 10000s of entities! and I'm packaging it with Electron for Steam as well.

You can try the game 100% free here [https://www.zombiesperminute.com](https://www.zombiesperminute.com) 

(any feedback is welcome as I would like to polish the experience as much as possible, thank you so much!) 

There is also a X thread when you can see all steps of development [https://x.com/NicolasZu/status/2028021321280442737?s=20](https://x.com/NicolasZu/status/2028021321280442737?s=20)

I would be happy to answer any of your questions!

Basically being realistic of the model limitations and apply critical thinking to what its making. A lot of "Vibe Coders" just throw some prompt and pray for something good to be generated and when it's bad they:  
\- Don't know how to fix it  
\- Or just don't fix it 'cuz they don't have now the standars for the thing that they are coding.

With AI you can quickly oscillate from 200% to -200% of productivity so you gotta be always understanding your code and don't get "Aww awesome its doing all the work for me" 'cuz those are the moments when you either low your expectations or your gonna have to spend the next two hours rebuilding something that AI mistunderstood or straightaway just broke

replies.author: RetroFootballManager
replies.body:
I write detailed implementation plans as my prompts for every feature. I write an extremely detailed game design document. I create the systems including how systems interact, how formulas work, the flow of each system into another… you know… the exact thing you would do if you were coding it yourself but a bit more detailed because I strictly state implementation methods where normally I wouldn’t do that because I’d just decide when I got to it.

I then use a whole agent system with agents with different responsibilities and have them review the document and implementation plans.

I iron through their findings and change things I believe are issues and leave things I don’t. I then have an agent create epics with tickets. I have an architect take the ticket, use my initial plan and propose the actual implementation. I review that implementation. A different agent then goes through a TDD style development based on that plan which gets reviewed by the main agent once it’s done. I then review it and have a QA Agent run unit tests and make sure everything is covered as designed. It then gets merged. 

This is the basic system. It’s a lot of work still but it’s also much more efficient than doing it all alone. It also helps me slow down in a way and make sure my design choices make sense before coding them.
